extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (campaign planners, fund-raising specialists, nonprofit communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, executing, and evaluating promotional, fund-raising, and public-communication campaigns, with emphasis on choosing objectives by type of public, campaign techniques, and evaluation measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Program (fund-raising campaign type)
rubrics_metrics.description: A massive effort to raise a targeted amount of money for a major building or similar project within a specified period of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: university cultural center, church or hospital building projects. These are long, targeted drives that require focused planning and timelines (e.g., Iowa State University's C. Y. Stephens cultural center example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaigns for Annual Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring campaigns to raise funds needed for annual operating expenses of an organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be conducted year-round (alumni programs), in one intensive community drive (Community Chest/United Givers Fund), or via direct mail/telethon (public TV). Examples: American Cancer Society, Red Cross, alumni annual funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising Funds from Foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Soliciting funds from private foundations for specific projects by researching suitable foundations, writing proposals, and conferring with foundation representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fund-raisers must research foundations (roughly 26,000 available), prepare formal proposals, and follow up with foundation contacts to present or clarify projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeking Corporate Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Soliciting donations or sponsorship from corporations, typically those located in an organization's geographic area or with interests aligned to the organization's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques mirror foundation solicitation; may include matching gifts by employers. Target corporations with local ties or specific interest in the program/department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred Giving Programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs that solicit gifts which provide tax advantages to donors by giving part or all of their estate or transferring assets during their lifetime in exchange for retained life income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes wills, lifetime transfers, gifts of property or equipment; used to attract donors who seek tax or income benefits from giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-Raising Techniques (media and interpersonal tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of tactical methods used to secure donations and maintain donor relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes media relations, letter writing and direct mail solicitation, writing proposals to foundations/corporations, intensive campaigns (media promotion, staged events, telethons, celebrity support), providing ongoing information to donors (magazines, newsletters, annual reports), speeches to donor groups, and interpersonal contacts with key prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical Segments of a Fund-Raising Program
rubrics_metrics.description: Core procedural/strategic steps that structure a fund-raising program: establishing objectives; identifying/researching prospects; writing a case statement; cultivating donors; soliciting gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish organizational objectives to determine the appropriate fund-raising program; use research to identify 'natural prospects'; write a persuasive case statement showing why funds are needed and why donations matter (not 'begging'); cultivate prospects via visits, events, and information; finally, solicit the gift. Evaluation and record-keeping are also essential segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of Research and Record-Keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Fund-raisers should conduct research to identify prospects and keep extensive records of prospects and donations for evaluation and future targeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although many fund-raisers historically do little research, formative research and discriminant analysis can identify characteristics that separate donors from non-donors and improve targeting and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Discriminant Analysis to Identify Active Publics
rubrics_metrics.description: A statistical technique to determine which characteristics distinguish donors (or likely buyers/attendees) from non-donors, enabling focused solicitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kathleen Kelly's study of alumni used discriminant analysis to identify those most likely to give, allowing fund-raisers to spend solicitation money more efficiently. Key discriminators may include income, past giving, dues payments, and perceived constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint Recognition (obstacle analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and address perceived constraints that prevent interested publics from donating or behaving as desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research often shows people may recognize a problem but perceive constraints (e.g., lack of money, low perceived impact of small gifts). Effective campaigns must either target unconstrained publics or reduce constraints (discounts, payment options, demonstrating impact). Case example: young alumni aware of needs but constrained financially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing a Persuasive Case Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A written statement that explains clearly why the organization needs funds and why prospects should contribute, making the appeal appear substantive rather than mere begging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overwhelming technical detail (e.g., schematic equipment lists with unfamiliar terms); present donor-relevant impacts (what a gift will accomplish), and demonstrate that a contribution will matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Communication Campaign Objective Selection by Public Type
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose campaign objectives based on the nature of the target public: behavior-change objectives for active publics, and exposure/retention/acceptance objectives for passive publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If behavior (e.g., filling seats, selling products, raising funds) is essential, communicate to active publics already predisposed to act. For passive, low-involvement publics (e.g., seat-belt campaigns), realistic objectives are message exposure, retention, and acceptance; behavior change will require complementary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model Choice for Campaigns (four models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and choose among the four public relations models (press agent/marketing-style publicity, public information, two-way asymmetric research-informed persuasion, two-way symmetric/dialogue) as appropriate to campaign aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many campaigns historically used press-agent or public-information models; more effective campaigns use research-informed asymmetric approaches or two-way symmetric approaches to tailor messages and involve publics. Use model selection to determine strategy and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Social Marketing and Marketing Strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply commercial marketing and social-marketing strategies to public communication campaigns that seek acceptance of social ideas or practices rather than sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns for behavior reform (e.g., antismoking, family planning, pollution prevention) use marketing techniques—audience research, segmentation, positioning, repeated messaging—and may aim to get people to stop harmful behaviors as social marketing objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three 'E's' for Behavior-Change Campaigns (education, enforcement, engineering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral-change campaigns should combine communication (education) with enforcement (laws, sanctions) and engineering (environmental/structural changes) to create conditions that enable desired behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: U.S. Forest Service wildfire prevention used education, enforcement of fire laws, and engineering (physical constraints around campfires). Chessie System railroad combined education, enforcement, and engineering to reduce grade-crossing accidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpersonal Support as Essential Backup
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpersonal group support (e.g., Alcoholics Anonymous, MADD, Weight Watchers) is often necessary to help individuals change entrenched behaviors after a campaign raises awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns can raise problem recognition, but individuals often need group support, training, or organized follow-up to change behavior; interpersonal networks increase likelihood of sustained change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servicing People’s Information Needs (two-way symmetric planning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan campaigns by asking target publics what information they need and what information they used when facing the problem, then design messages and services to meet those perceived needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A symmetric approach solicits audience input in formative research so campaigns provide relevant, usable information rather than only top-down messaging; this increases relevance and potential effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling Objectives for Passive/Low-Involvement Publics
rubrics_metrics.description: For passive or low-involvement publics, scale down behavioral expectations and focus objectives on exposure, message retention, and acceptance, recognizing that only a small fraction may move to active information seeking and behavior change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mendelsohn's work suggests information campaigns can increase knowledge and some eventual behavior change; Grunig-Ipes study showed campaigns primarily put issues on passive publics' agenda with limited behavior change without additional supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion Strategies for Low-Involvement Products
rubrics_metrics.description: Use frequent exposure (advertising, publicity, staged events) to create name recognition and habitual purchase behavior for low-cost or low-involvement products where brand differences are not strongly perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television advertising, publicity stunts (blimps, hot-air balloons), and repetition increase recall and habit formation; these strategies work because consumers often buy by simple recognition rather than deliberation for low-involvement purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation: Measure Multiple Objectives (behavior + intermediate effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate campaigns not only by final behavioral outcomes but also by intermediate objectives such as exposure, message retention, message acceptance, and coorientational effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring only behavior can make a campaign appear to fail when it achieved maximal effect for a given public. Use measures described elsewhere in the book (e.g., sampling approaches in Chapter 9) and include formative, process, and outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure Coorientational Effects (symmetric evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For symmetric and two-way campaigns, evaluate changes in mutual understanding (coorientation) between the organization and publics as part of campaign effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coorientational measures assess alignment of perceptions and can be important outcomes for campaigns that aim to improve relationships or mutual understanding rather than only behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Complementary Techniques to Remove Constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: To move people beyond awareness, use strategies (engineering changes, enforcement actions, interpersonal support, incentives/discounts) that reduce or remove constraints preventing the desired behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: family discounts to reduce cost constraints for sports attendance; enforcement and engineering for traffic safety; MADD providing interpersonal support for drunk-driving campaign participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect Limited Effects of Information Alone on Behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume information campaigns alone will produce widespread behavior change; information can raise problem recognition and knowledge but often is insufficient to alter behavior across a mass public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical research (Hyman & Sheatsley; Bauer) shows limited behavioral impact; Mendelsohn and later studies show information can increase knowledge and some behavior when combined with research-based targeting and complementary measures.
